cleaned_caption:
Quant math looks like one giant pile you have to swallow whole. It isn’t. It’s a sequence, and the sequence is most of the difficulty.

This is the order I’d follow if I started from zero today. Nine topics, from high school algebra up to calibrating a volatility surface. Foundations, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistical inference, computational methods, optimization, stochastic processes, pricing.

Three things in here that other roadmaps get wrong. Optimization needs nothing past linear algebra and belongs early, not in year three. Measure theory is the second pass through stochastic calculus, not the prerequisite for it. And Bayesian methods aren’t optional, because you never have the sample size the frequentist story assumes.

The catch: reading all nine takes close to two years, and at the end of it you still have nothing to show anyone. Nobody gets hired for having read Shreve. Knowing the order is half of it. Applying it is the other half, and that’s the half that decides it.
